title: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
summary: How an OS virtualizes the CPU and memory (traps, scheduling, paging, page replacement), coordinates threads (locks, condition variables, deadlock) and keeps files consistent across crashes, with OSTEP's examples.
outcomes: Explain how traps, the trap table and the timer interrupt let an OS run programs directly yet keep control
Compute turnaround and response time for FIFO, SJF, STCF and round robin schedules
Translate an address through linear and two-level page tables and compute TLB hit rates for an access pattern
Trace a page fault and compare OPT, FIFO, LRU and clock replacement on a reference string
Explain why x++ on shared data races and why locks need atomic instructions such as test-and-set
Order threads with condition variables and semaphores, and recognize atomicity, order and deadlock bugs
Compute disk I/O time and count the disk reads a path lookup through directories and inodes costs
Explain how fsck and data and ordered journaling keep multi-block updates crash-safe

blocks.md: An operating system (OS) has three jobs, which OSTEP calls the three easy pieces. OSTEP is short for *Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces*, the free textbook by Remzi and Andrea Arpaci-Dusseau that this course follows. The three pieces are **virtualization** (make one CPU and one memory look like many private ones), **concurrency** (let many things happen at once without corrupting shared data) and **persistence** (keep data safe on disks across crashes). Lessons 1 to 4 cover virtualization, 5 to 7 concurrency and 8 to 10 persistence, using the same examples as the book so you can read along.

This course stays at the level of the book's mechanisms. Two later courses carry them into Linux: *Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch* (the process lifecycle and the Linux scheduler) and *Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB* (the process memory map, malloc, page reclaim and swap).

The first abstraction is the **process**: a running program. Its state is its memory (the *address space*: code, heap, stack), its registers (including the program counter, PC, which holds the address of the next instruction to run, and the stack pointer, which holds the address of the top of the stack) and its open files. The OS keeps a per-process record of this state, often called a process control block (PCB), in a *process list*.

A process is always in one of three simplified states:

- **Running**: executing instructions on a CPU.
- **Ready**: could run, but the OS has chosen to run something else.
- **Blocked**: waiting for some event, such as a disk read finishing, so it cannot run yet. When the disk is done it raises an **interrupt**: a hardware signal that makes the CPU pause what it is running and jump to an OS handler.

Moving from ready to running is called being *scheduled*; running to ready is being *descheduled*.

blocks.title: Two processes moving through the state machine

scenes.caption: Time 1 to 3 (OSTEP Figure 4.4): Process0 (P0) runs on the single CPU while Process1 (P1) waits in Ready.
Time 4: P0 initiates an I/O and becomes Blocked. The CPU would sit idle, so the OS schedules P1 instead.
Time 7: the disk finishes and raises an interrupt. The OS moves P0 to Ready, not straight to Running: P1 keeps the CPU.
Time 9: P1 has finished, so P0 is scheduled and runs to completion at time 10. Overlapping P0's I/O with P1's computation kept the CPU busy.

blocks.md: UNIX creates processes with two calls. `fork()` makes an almost exact copy of the caller: same code, a private copy of memory and registers. The only difference is the return value: the parent gets the child's process ID (PID), the child gets 0. `exec()` then replaces the current program with a new one, and `wait()` lets a parent block until a child exits. A UNIX shell runs the commands you type with exactly this fork, exec, wait sequence.

blocks.title: Tracing fork() and wait() (OSTEP p2.c)

scenes.caption: One process (PID 29266) prints hello. So far nothing unusual.
fork() returns twice: once in the parent with the child's PID, once in the new child with 0. Two processes now run this same code.
Suppose the scheduler runs the parent first. It calls wait(NULL) and becomes Blocked until its child exits.
The child takes the rc == 0 branch, prints, and exits.
wait() returns the child's PID and the parent prints last. Without wait() either order could appear; with it the output is deterministic.

blocks.md: Now the core question: how does the OS run a process fast but stay in control? The fast part is **direct execution**: load the program and jump to `main()`, so it runs natively on the CPU. The *limited* part needs hardware help. The CPU has a **user mode**, where restricted operations such as I/O raise an exception (the hardware stops the instruction and hands control to the OS), and a **kernel mode**, where the OS can do anything. The **kernel** is the core of the OS, the part that runs in kernel mode.

A program asks for a privileged service with a **system call**. The C library puts a system-call number in a register and executes a **trap** instruction, which raises the privilege level and jumps into the kernel. The program cannot pick the jump target: at boot the kernel installs a **trap table** telling the hardware which handler runs for each event. When the work is done, **return-from-trap** drops back to user mode.

That solves restricted operations, but not a process that loops forever and never makes a system call. If the OS only waits for system calls to get control back, which OSTEP calls the *cooperative* approach, such a process keeps the CPU forever. The fix is a **timer interrupt**: a device, started by the OS at boot, that interrupts the CPU every few milliseconds and runs an OS handler. At that point the OS can do a **context switch**: save the current process's registers and restore another's. Taking the CPU away from a running process like this is called **preemption**. The span a process runs between two switches is its **time slice**.

Each process also has a **kernel stack**, a separate stack in kernel memory that the kernel uses while it handles a trap or interrupt for that process. A timer-driven switch therefore saves registers in two places. When the interrupt fires, the hardware pushes the process's user registers onto its kernel stack. Then the OS switch routine saves the kernel's own registers (the ones it was using while running the handler) into the process structure, the PCB.

blocks.title: Limited direct execution with a timer interrupt

scenes.caption: At boot, in kernel mode, the OS tells the hardware where its trap handlers live and starts the interrupt timer. Both are privileged operations.
Process A runs directly on the CPU in user mode. The OS is not running at all, so it cannot act until something hands control back.

add.label: user mode, jump to A's PC

scenes.caption: The timer fires. Hardware saves A's registers onto A's kernel stack, switches to kernel mode and jumps to the timer handler.
The scheduler picks B. switch() saves A's kernel registers into A's process structure, restores B's, and switches to B's kernel stack.
return-from-trap now restores B's registers, because the stack it pops from is B's. The CPU drops to user mode and resumes B where it left off.
Later B makes a system call. It traps into the handler chosen at boot, the OS does the work, and return-from-trap resumes B after the trap.

blocks.md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

A system call is not just a function call. It looks like one because the C library wraps it, but inside is a trap that changes privilege level, and the kernel, not the caller, decides which code runs.

blocks.question: Under a purely cooperative OS (no timer interrupt), a process enters `while (1) {}` and never makes a system call. What happens?
options: The OS never runs again on that CPU; in practice the machine must be rebooted
The OS notices after one time slice and preempts it
The trap table automatically jumps to the scheduler after a while
The process is killed because infinite loops are privileged operations
blocks.explain: With no timer interrupt, the OS only regains control when the process makes a system call or does something illegal. An infinite loop does neither, so the OS cannot run. OSTEP notes the only recourse is to reboot. This is exactly why the timer interrupt exists.

blocks.question: Why must the instruction that installs the trap table be privileged?
options: Because it is slow and should run only at boot
Because the trap table is stored on disk
Because a user process could otherwise point system calls and interrupts at its own code and take over the machine
Because user programs do not know the system-call numbers
blocks.explain: The trap table decides which code runs in kernel mode on every trap and interrupt. If a user program could install its own, it would run arbitrary code with full privilege, defeating all protection. So, like starting the timer, it is restricted to kernel mode.

lessons.title: CPU scheduling: turnaround time versus response time

blocks.md: The timer gives the OS a chance to switch processes; the **scheduler** decides *which* one runs. To compare policies we need metrics. **Turnaround time** is completion time minus arrival time; it matters for batch jobs, which run with no user waiting on them. **Response time** is the time from arrival to the first time the job runs; it matters for interactive programs.

blocks.tex: T_{\text{turnaround}} = T_{\text{completion}} - T_{\text{arrival}} \qquad T_{\text{response}} = T_{\text{firstrun}} - T_{\text{arrival}}

blocks.md: OSTEP's running example: three jobs A, B and C arrive at time 0. A needs 100 seconds of CPU, B and C need 10 each. **FIFO** (first in, first out) runs them in arrival order, A first. **SJF** (shortest job first) runs the shortest first. Both are non-preemptive: once started, a job runs to completion. A preemptive scheduler may stop a running job to run another; the figure below also shows STCF, the preemptive version of SJF, explained right after it.

blocks.prompt: Under FIFO, with A (100 s) arriving just before B and C (10 s each), what is the average turnaround time? And under SJF?
blocks.reveal: FIFO: A finishes at 100, B at 110, C at 120, so the average is $(100+110+120)/3 = 110$ s. SJF runs B and C first: they finish at 10 and 20, A at 120, so the average is $(10+20+120)/3 = 50$ s. Same work, less than half the average wait. Short jobs stuck behind a long one is called the **convoy effect**.

blocks.title: FIFO, SJF and STCF on the same three jobs

scenes.caption: FIFO, all arrive at 0: A hogs the CPU for 100 s. Turnaround: A 100, B 110, C 120, average 110 s.
SJF, all arrive at 0: B and C go first. Turnaround: B 10, C 20, A 120, average 50 s. With simultaneous arrivals SJF is optimal for average turnaround.
Now B and C arrive at t = 10, after A started. Non-preemptive SJF cannot stop A. Turnaround: A 100, B 100, C 110, average 103.33 s. The convoy is back.
STCF (preemptive SJF): at t = 10 it preempts A, whose 90 s remaining is longest. Turnaround: A 120, B 10, C 20, average 50 s. Response: 0, 0, 10, average 3.33 s.

blocks.md: **STCF** (shortest time-to-completion first) adds preemption: whenever a job arrives, run whichever job has the least time *remaining*. It needs the timer and context switch from lesson 1. But all these policies are bad for response time: if three 5-second jobs arrive together, SJF makes the third wait 10 seconds before it runs even once.

**Round robin (RR)** fixes response time: run each job for a **time slice** (also called a quantum), then switch to the next job in the queue. The slice must be a multiple of the timer-interrupt period, so with a 10 ms timer it could be 10, 20 or 30 ms.

blocks.title: SJF versus round robin on three 5-second jobs

scenes.caption: SJF (ties broken A, B, C): response times 0, 5, 10 (average 5 s); turnaround 5, 10, 15 (average 10 s).
RR with a 1 s slice: every job starts within 2 s, so average response is 1 s. But A finishes at 13, B at 14, C at 15: average turnaround 14 s, worse than SJF's 10.

blocks.md: Each switch costs time: saving and restoring registers, plus colder CPU caches, TLB and branch predictors for the incoming job. The TLB is a hardware cache of address translations (lesson 3), and the branch predictor is hardware that guesses which way upcoming branches go. All three were filled by the previous job, so they are *cold* for the new one: it misses until they refill. OSTEP's example: with a 1 ms switch cost, a 10 ms slice wastes roughly 10% of the CPU, and a 100 ms slice under 1%. That rough figure is just cost over slice, 1/10. The plot below uses a slightly more exact model. Call the switch cost $c$ and the slice $q$. Each round, the CPU runs a job for $q$ ms and then spends $c$ ms switching, so a round lasts $q + c$ and the fraction lost is overhead $= c/(q+c)$. With $c = 1$, that is $1/11$, about 9 percent, for a 10 ms slice and $1/101$, about 1 percent, for 100 ms.

blocks.title: Context-switch overhead versus time-slice length

scenes.caption: With c = 1 ms, a 10 ms slice loses about 9% to switching and a 100 ms slice about 1%. Longer slices amortize the fixed cost.
Simplified model: real switch costs also include refilling caches and the TLB. If the effective cost rises to 3 ms, short slices become very expensive.

blocks.md:
Real schedulers do not know job lengths. OSTEP's answer is the **multi-level feedback queue (MLFQ)**: several queues, one per priority level (multi-level), where a job's observed behavior is fed back to change its priority (feedback). Its rules, with the **allotment** being how much CPU time a job may use at one level before it is demoted:

1. Higher priority runs first; equal priorities share the CPU round robin.
2. New jobs start at the top priority (assume a job is short and interactive).
3. Once a job uses up its time allotment at a level, it moves down one level, no matter how many times it gave up the CPU.
4. Every period S (a time span the OS designer picks), move all jobs back to the top, so long jobs do not starve: without this, a steady stream of short interactive jobs at the top could keep a long job at the bottom from ever running.

OSTEP notes that BSD UNIX derivatives (BSD is the Berkeley Software Distribution, the UNIX line from the University of California, Berkeley), Solaris and Windows NT and later use forms of MLFQ as their base scheduler.

No policy wins on every metric. SJF and STCF minimize average turnaround but give long waits before a job first runs; round robin gives fast response but stretches every job's completion. Choosing a scheduler means choosing which metric you care about.

blocks.question: Three 5-second jobs arrive together. You switch from SJF to round robin with a 1 s slice. What happens to average turnaround and average response time?
options: Both improve
Turnaround gets worse (10 s to 14 s) and response gets better (5 s to 1 s)
Turnaround improves and response gets worse
Both stay the same because the total work is unchanged
blocks.explain: RR starts every job almost immediately, so average response drops from 5 s to 1 s. But it interleaves the jobs, so all of them finish near the end: 13, 14 and 15 s, averaging 14 s versus SJF's 10 s. Fairness over short time scales costs turnaround.

blocks.question: A job in MLFQ runs for 9 ms of a 10 ms allotment, then issues a tiny I/O, and repeats forever. Under the final rule (allotment counts total use at a level), what happens?
options: It stays at top priority forever because it always yields before its allotment ends
It is demoted once its total CPU use at that level reaches the allotment, even across many short bursts
It is killed for gaming the scheduler
It is promoted because it does I/O
blocks.explain: An older version of the rule reset the allotment whenever a job gave up the CPU, so this pattern could monopolize the CPU. The refined allotment rule (item 3 in the list above, Rule 4 in OSTEP) tracks total time used at a level, whether in one long burst or many short ones, so the gaming job is demoted.

lessons.title: Virtual memory: paging, page tables and the TLB

blocks.md: The second thing the OS virtualizes is memory. Every process sees its own **address space** starting at 0, and every pointer you used in C is a **virtual address**. The hardware's memory management unit (MMU) translates each one into a **physical address** on every load, store and instruction fetch. This gives isolation (a process cannot even name another's memory) and lets the OS place memory wherever it likes.

**Paging** chops the address space into fixed-size **pages** and physical memory into same-size **page frames**. A per-process **page table** maps each virtual page number (VPN) to a physical frame number (PFN). The low bits of an address, the **offset**, select a byte inside the page and are never translated.

Recall OSTEP's tiny example, which the earlier course *How a computer runs a program* worked bit by bit: a 64-byte address space with 16-byte pages, a page table mapping virtual page (VP) 0 to frame 3, VP 1 to frame 7, VP 2 to frame 5 and VP 3 to frame 2, and virtual address 21 (VPN 1, offset 5) landing at physical address $7 \times 16 + 5 = 117$. Translation swaps the VPN for the PFN and copies the offset unchanged.

Each **page table entry (PTE)** holds the PFN plus bits the OS and hardware use: a **valid** bit (unused regions of a sparse address space are invalid, and touching them traps to the OS), **protection** bits (read, write, execute), a **present** bit (in memory or swapped to disk), a **dirty** bit and a **reference** (accessed) bit. When memory runs short, the OS can copy rarely used pages out to a swap area on disk, and the present bit records which pages it has moved there (the next lesson follows that path). The hardware sets the dirty bit when the page is written, so the OS knows it must copy the page back to disk before reusing its frame. It sets the reference bit on any access, which tells the OS which pages are in use when it picks one to evict. On x86 the present bit doubles as valid, and the U/S (user/supervisor) bit decides whether user mode may touch the page.

blocks.prompt: A 32-bit address space with 4 KB pages and 4-byte PTEs uses a simple linear (array) page table. How big is one process's page table? And for 100 processes?
blocks.reveal: 4 KB pages need 12 offset bits, leaving a 20-bit VPN, so $2^{20}$ entries (about a million). At 4 bytes each that is $2^{20} \times 4 = 4$ MB per process, and 400 MB for 100 processes, just for translations. This is why real systems use **multi-level page tables**, below.

blocks.caption: One entry per possible virtual page, valid or not.

blocks.md: A **multi-level page table** chops the linear table into page-sized pieces and adds a **page directory**, an array with one **page directory entry** (PDE) per piece. A PDE holds a valid bit and the frame number where that piece lives. If every PTE in a piece would be invalid, the piece is simply not allocated and its PDE is marked invalid. Space now grows with the memory a process actually uses, and each piece fits in one page, so the OS can place it in any free frame.

OSTEP's worked example: a 16 KB address space with 64-byte pages. That is a 14-bit virtual address: 6 offset bits ($2^6 = 64$) and an 8-bit VPN, so 256 virtual pages. VPs 0 and 1 hold code, 4 and 5 the heap, 254 and 255 the stack; the rest are unused. A linear table needs 256 PTEs of 4 bytes, 1 KB, which is 16 pages of 16 PTEs each. So the directory needs 16 entries: the top 4 bits of the VPN index the directory, the next 4 bits index a page of PTEs.

blocks.title: Two-level translation of virtual address 0x3F80

scenes.caption: 0x3F80 is 11 1111 1000 0000 in binary. Top 4 bits: directory index. Next 4: index within a page of PTEs. Low 6: offset. Only 3 pages hold the table: the directory and two pages of PTEs.
Directory index 1111 = 15. That PDE is valid and says the page of PTEs covering VPNs 240 to 255 lives in frame 101. The 14 PDEs in between are invalid: no PTE pages for them.
PTE index 1110 = 14, in the page at frame 101. That PTE is valid, read-write, and maps VPN 254 (the stack) to frame 55. That is the second memory load of the walk.
Physical address = 55 x 64 + 0 = 3520, or 0x0DC0: frame 55 concatenated with offset 000000. Same offset, new frame, found with two loads instead of one.
For comparison, the code and heap: VPNs 0 to 15 share directory entry 0, whose page of PTEs at frame 100 maps VP 0 to 10, VP 1 to 23, VP 4 to 80 and VP 5 to 59.

blocks.prompt: How much memory does this two-level table use, compared with the 1 KB linear table?
blocks.reveal: Three pages of 64 bytes, 192 bytes in all: the directory (16 PDEs of 4 bytes) plus the two pages of PTEs that hold valid mappings. The linear table needs all 16 pages. For a 32-bit or 64-bit address space, where nearly all of the space is unused, the saving is far larger.

blocks.md: The price is time. On a TLB miss the hardware now needs two memory loads (the PDE, then the PTE) instead of one; on a TLB hit the cost is identical. OSTEP calls this a time-space trade-off. Real x86-64 uses the same idea with 4 levels, and the hardware finds the root of the tree through the CR3 (control register 3) register; the earlier course *How a computer runs a program* already walked that 4-level tree for a real address.

Paging has a speed problem too: every access first needs a PTE from memory. The fix is a **translation lookaside buffer (TLB)**, a small, fast hardware cache of recent VPN to PFN translations inside the MMU. On a **TLB hit** translation is nearly free; on a **TLB miss** the page table is consulted (by the hardware on x86, or by an OS trap handler on software-managed TLBs such as the MIPS processor family) and the TLB is filled. A small TLB works because programs show **locality**. Spatial locality: after touching an address, a program soon touches nearby ones, often on the same page. Temporal locality: it touches the same address again soon.

blocks.title: TLB hits while summing a 10-integer array

scenes.caption: OSTEP's setup: 4-byte ints starting at virtual address 100, 8-bit addresses, 16-byte pages (VPN = address / 16). The TLB starts empty.
a[0] at address 100 is on VPN 6: miss, the page table is walked and the TLB filled. a[1] and a[2] are on the same page: hits.
a[3] at 112 starts VPN 7: one miss, then a[4] to a[6] hit.
a[7] at 128 starts VPN 8: miss, then two hits. Total 7 hits out of 10: a 70% hit rate on the very first pass, thanks to spatial locality.
Loop over the array again soon after: if the TLB still holds VPNs 6, 7 and 8, all 10 accesses hit. That is temporal locality.

blocks.md: Bigger pages mean fewer TLB misses for dense data: with 32-byte pages the same loop would miss less, and with typical 4 KB pages a sequential scan misses only once per page. Programs that jump randomly across many pages are the ones that suffer.
The offset is never translated, and the page table is per process. Two processes can use the same virtual address 21 and reach completely different physical bytes; that is the isolation, not a bug.

blocks.question: Using the same 64-byte address space and page table (VP 0 to frame 3, VP 1 to 7, VP 2 to 5, VP 3 to 2), what physical address does virtual address 40 map to?
blocks.explain: 40 is 101000 in binary: VPN 10 = 2 and offset 1000 = 8. VP 2 lives in frame 5, so the physical address is 5 x 16 + 8 = 88. Answer 40 forgets translation; 72 would be frame 4; 117 is the earlier example.

blocks.question: Why does a multi-level page table make a TLB miss more expensive than a linear page table?
options: The TLB must be flushed after each lookup
The walk needs a load from the page directory and then from the page of PTEs, instead of one load
Multi-level tables are stored on disk
Each level must be translated by the TLB first
blocks.explain: A linear table needs one memory reference to fetch the PTE. A two-level table first reads the page directory entry to find the right page of the page table, then reads the PTE: two loads. It is a time-space trade-off; on a TLB hit the cost is identical.

blocks.question: In the same 16 KB example, a program touches virtual page 100 (binary 0110 0100). What happens?
options: The hardware reads the PTE at index 4 of the page at frame 100
The PDE at index 6 is invalid, so the hardware raises an exception without reading any page of PTEs
The MMU allocates a new page of PTEs for that region
It maps to frame 100, the first valid entry
blocks.explain: The directory index is the top 4 bits, 0110 = 6, and only PDEs 0 and 15 are valid. An invalid PDE means no PTE in that 16-page region is valid, so the access traps right away. Allocating page-table pages is the OS's job, not the MMU's.

lessons.title: Beyond physical memory: page faults, swapping and replacement

blocks.md: So far every page of every process sat in physical memory. Real programs together want more. OSTEP's tiny picture: a physical memory of 4 frames and a **swap space** of 8 page-sized blocks on disk. Processes 0, 1 and 2 each have some pages in memory and the rest in swap; process 3 has all its pages in swap, so it cannot be running. Swap space is disk space reserved for moving pages out of memory (swapping out) and back in (swapping in). Code pages need no swap: they can be read again from the program's file on disk.

The PTE's **present bit** says where the page is. When the hardware finds a valid PTE with present = 0, it raises an exception and the OS's **page-fault handler** runs. OSTEP notes the name is odd: the access is perfectly legal, so it is really a *page miss*. It is called a fault because the hardware handles it exactly like an illegal access, by trapping to the OS. An access to an *invalid* page, by contrast, is a real error, and the OS usually terminates the process.

blocks.title: Servicing a page fault, step by step

scenes.caption: The process loads from virtual page P. The TLB misses, so the hardware walks the page table and finds the PTE: valid, but present = 0. The page is on disk.
The hardware cannot fetch from disk itself, so it raises a page-fault exception, just as for an illegal access, and the OS's page-fault handler runs.
The OS takes a free frame, or first evicts a page (writing it out if dirty). It reads the page's swap address from the PTE and issues the read. The process is Blocked.
A disk read takes milliseconds, so the OS runs other ready processes meanwhile. When the read finishes, the disk raises an interrupt.
The OS marks the page present, records frame F in the PTE and makes the process Ready. When it runs, the faulting instruction is retried.
The retry misses in the TLB again; this time the walk finds a present page and fills the TLB. One more retry hits, and the load finally completes.

blocks.md: The disk address of a swapped-out page can be kept in the PTE itself, in the bits that would hold the PFN. Page faults are handled by the OS even on hardware-managed TLBs, for two reasons OSTEP gives: a disk read is so slow that the extra instructions cost nothing by comparison, and the hardware would otherwise have to understand swap space and disk I/O.

The OS does not wait until memory is completely full. With a **low watermark** (LW) and a **high watermark** (HW): when fewer than LW pages are free, a background thread evicts pages until HW pages are free, then sleeps. It is called the swap daemon or page daemon. *Daemon*, an old word for a background process, goes back to MIT's Project MAC in the 1960s; Fernando Corbató, who led the time-sharing work there, said the team took it from Maxwell's daemon of physics, an imaginary agent that works tirelessly in the background. Evicting many pages at once also lets the OS *cluster* writes into one larger, cheaper disk write.

Physical memory is now a cache for pages, and the **replacement policy** decides which page to evict. How much does a miss cost? OSTEP computes the **average memory access time** (AMAT): every access pays the memory cost $T_M$, and the fraction $P_{miss}$ that miss also pays the disk cost $T_D$.

blocks.caption: With T_M = 100 ns and T_D = 10 ms, a 0.1% miss rate gives 100 ns + 0.001 x 10 ms = 10.1 microseconds.

blocks.title: Average memory access time when misses go to disk

scenes.caption: OSTEP's numbers: 100 ns memory, 10 ms disk. A 10% miss rate gives about 1 ms per access; 0.1% gives 10.1 us, still 100 times slower than memory.
Only around a 0.001% miss rate (one access in 100,000) does the average fall to 0.2 us, twice the memory cost. Slide T_D down to see how a faster swap device moves the curve.

blocks.md: Which page should go? Laszlo Belady, an IBM researcher, showed the optimal policy in 1966; which Belady called MIN and OSTEP calls OPT: evict the page that will be used **furthest in the future**. It needs knowledge of the future, so no real OS can run it, but it is the yardstick for every real policy. **FIFO** (first in, first out) evicts the page that arrived earliest. **LRU** (least recently used) evicts the page untouched for the longest time, betting on temporal locality from lesson 3.

blocks.title: OPT, FIFO and LRU on OSTEP's reference stream, 3 frames

scenes.caption: Eleven page accesses, a memory that holds 3 pages, starting empty. The first three accesses miss whatever the policy: these are cold-start (compulsory) misses.
OPT at access 3: the future uses 0 next, then 1, and 2 last, so evict 2. At the later access to 2, evict 3 (0 would also do). Result: 6 hits, 5 misses, 54.5%. No policy can do better.
FIFO evicts the page that came in first (cache listed oldest first). At access 3 that is 0, which is needed next, then 1, needed soon after. Result: 4 hits, 36.4%.
LRU evicts the least recently used page (cache listed least recent first). At access 3 that is 2, since 0 and 1 were just used. History guesses well here: 6 hits, matching OPT.

blocks.prompt: Belady and colleagues found a stream that surprises people: 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Under FIFO, how many misses with 3 frames, and with 4 frames?
blocks.reveal: 3 frames: 9 misses. 4 frames: **10 misses**. More memory made FIFO worse! This is **Belady's anomaly**. LRU cannot suffer it, because it has the *stack property*: a cache of N + 1 pages always holds what a cache of N pages would hold, so adding memory never adds a miss. On this stream LRU gets 10 misses with 3 frames and 8 with 4.

blocks.md: LRU has its own worst case. OSTEP's **looping-sequential** workload touches pages 0 to 49 in order, again and again. The page LRU or FIFO evicts is always the one needed soonest, so with a 49-page cache both get a 0% hit rate; Random does noticeably better. Policies that resist this are called *scan resistant*. And perfect LRU is too expensive anyway: it must update a list on every memory access, and with 4 GB of 4 KB pages, finding the oldest of about a million pages on every eviction is far too slow.

So real systems approximate LRU with a hardware **use bit** (also called the reference bit), first built in the Atlas, the first machine with paging. The hardware sets it to 1 whenever the page is read or written; only the OS clears it. Corbató's **clock algorithm** arranges the frames in a circle with a hand. At eviction time: if the page under the hand has use bit 1, clear it and advance (the page gets a second chance); if 0, evict it. A common refinement also checks the **dirty bit**: evicting a clean page is free, while a dirty one must first be written back to disk.

blocks.title: The clock algorithm picking victims

scenes.caption: A constructed example: four frames in a circle. Hardware set the use bit of every page touched recently; page 2's bit is 0. Page 5 faults and the clock hand points at frame 0.
Frame 0 has use bit 1: page 7 was used recently, so it gets a second chance. The OS clears the bit to 0 and moves the hand on.
Frame 1 has use bit 0: page 2 is the victim. It is clean, so no disk write is needed. Page 5 is read in, its use bit is set, and the hand moves on.
Page 6 faults with no accesses in between. Frames 2 and 3 have bit 1: cleared. Frame 0 still has 0, because page 7 was not touched during a whole lap. Evict 7, load 6.
The dirty-bit variant (simplified): on the next fault, pages 9 and 4 are both unused, but 9 is dirty and would need a disk write. Preferring unused and clean pages picks 4.

blocks.md: If the running processes' **working sets** (the pages each is actively using) together exceed memory, the system pages constantly and does little else. This is called **thrashing**; Peter Denning's 1970 survey of virtual memory is the classic analysis of it. Older systems used *admission control*: run fewer processes so that their working sets fit. Some versions of Linux instead run an out-of-memory (OOM) killer that picks a memory-hungry process and kills it. The later course *Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB* shows how Linux reclaims pages, with watermarks, the page cache and active and inactive lists.

Memory is a cache for pages, and a disk-backed miss costs about 100,000 memory accesses. A replacement policy tries to approximate OPT using the past: LRU in principle, the use bit and the clock algorithm in practice, preferring clean pages.

A page fault is not a bug. It is a legal access to a page that happens not to be in memory, and the program never notices except as a delay. A segmentation fault is different: an access to an invalid page, which the OS treats as an error.

blocks.question: A database scans a 50-page table in a loop, over and over, and has 49 frames for it. Which replacement policy gives the best hit rate?
options: LRU, because it keeps recently used pages
FIFO, because the scan is in arrival order
Random, because LRU and FIFO always evict the page needed next and hit 0% of the time
All three give the same hit rate
blocks.explain: In a loop larger than the cache, the least recently used page is exactly the one the loop needs next, so LRU (and FIFO, which evicts in the same order here) misses on every access. Random sometimes keeps the right pages and gets a non-zero hit rate. OPT would do better still.

blocks.question: With 100 ns memory and 10 ms disk, what is the average memory access time at a 1% miss rate?
options: About 100 microseconds
About 101 nanoseconds
About 10 milliseconds
About 1 microsecond
blocks.explain: AMAT = 100 ns + 0.01 x 10 ms = 0.1 us + 100 us = 100.1 us, a thousand times slower than memory. 101 ns would be the result if the miss cost were 100 ns, not 10 ms.

blocks.md: A **thread** is a second point of execution inside the same process. Each thread has its own registers, program counter and stack, but all threads share one address space, so they see the same globals and heap. Switching between threads works like a process context switch (state is saved in a thread control block), except the page table stays the same.
OSTEP's first threaded program starts two threads, each adding 1 to a shared global `counter` ten million times. The expected result is 20,000,000.

POSIX (Portable Operating System Interface, the standard that defines the UNIX programming interface) threads, the *pthreads* library, create a thread with `pthread_create(&t, attr, fn, arg)`: it starts running function `fn` with argument `arg`, and passing `NULL` for `attr` takes the default attributes (stack size, scheduling). `pthread_join(t, &ret)` blocks the caller until thread `t` finishes, like `wait()` for a child process. Here is OSTEP's program, with the book's error-checking wrappers removed:

blocks.caption: Build with `cc -pthread t1.c -o t1`. Two threads each add 1 ten million times to one shared global.

blocks.prompt: What do you expect when you run it, even on a single CPU?
blocks.reveal: Sometimes 20000000. But OSTEP's runs also printed **19345221** and then **19221041**: wrong, and different every time. Updates were lost. The outcome depends on exactly when the timer interrupt switched threads, which makes the result **indeterminate**.

blocks.md: On a multi-core machine it is worse, because both threads truly run at the same moment. Three runs of the program above on an Apple Silicon Mac printed counter values of 10,886,811, 10,948,175 and 10,663,408: nearly half the increments vanished. The rest of this lesson shows how a single update gets lost.

The C statement `counter = counter + 1` is not one machine step. The compiler emits three x86 instructions: load the value into register `eax`, add one to the register, store the register back. A timer interrupt can arrive between any two of them, and each thread has its own saved copy of `eax`.

blocks.title: How one increment gets lost (OSTEP Figure 26.7)

scenes.caption: Thread 1 loads counter (50) into its eax.
Thread 1 adds one: its eax is 51. Then the timer fires; the OS saves T1's registers, including eax = 51, and switches to Thread 2.
Thread 2 runs all three instructions: it loads 50, adds one, and stores 51. Memory now holds 51.
Another interrupt resumes Thread 1 at its third instruction. It stores its stale eax = 51 into memory.
Two increments ran, but counter went from 50 to 51, not 52. Repeat this millions of times and you get 19,345,221 instead of 20,000,000.

blocks.md: This is a **race condition** (here, a data race): the result depends on the timing of execution. A data race is the specific case where two threads access the same memory location at the same time, at least one of them writes, and nothing orders the accesses. Code that touches shared data and must not run in more than one thread at once is a **critical section**. What we want is **mutual exclusion**: while one thread is inside, others are kept out. Edsger Dijkstra, a Dutch computer scientist who won the Turing Award partly for this work, coined virtually all of these terms; Dijkstra's 1968 paper *Cooperating Sequential Processes* describes the problem clearly.
The tool for mutual exclusion is a **lock**. The POSIX threads library calls a lock a **mutex**, short for mutual exclusion. With POSIX threads you wrap the critical section:

blocks.caption: Only the thread holding the lock may run the increment, so the three instructions can no longer interleave.

blocks.md: How would you build `lock()` yourself? A first try uses a plain `flag` variable: spin (loop, checking it again and again) while `flag == 1`, then set `flag = 1`. This fails for the same reason the counter did: the *test* and the *set* are separate steps, and an interrupt can land between them.

blocks.title: A lock built from a plain flag lets both threads in

scenes.caption: flag starts at 0. Thread 1 calls lock() and tests the flag: it is 0, so T1 will fall out of the loop.
An interrupt switches to Thread 2 before T1 sets the flag. T2 also sees flag == 0 and sets it to 1. T2 is in the critical section.
T1 resumes at line 4 and sets flag = 1 too. Both threads are now inside the critical section: no mutual exclusion.

blocks.md: Hardware fixes this with an atomic instruction. **Test-and-set** (atomic exchange; `xchg` on x86) writes a new value and returns the old one as a single, indivisible step. A lock becomes: keep calling `TestAndSet(&flag, 1)` until it returns 0. Whoever sees 0 is the one thread that flipped the flag from free to held.

blocks.caption: OSTEP's spin lock (Figure 28.3). The C function only describes the semantics; real code uses the CPU's atomic instruction.

blocks.md: This **spin lock** is correct but not fair (a waiter may spin forever), and on one CPU it can waste a lot: if N threads compete for the lock and the holder is preempted, each of the other N - 1 threads may spin away a whole time slice. Real locks therefore sleep (block, giving up the CPU until another thread wakes them) instead of spinning when the lock is **contended**, that is, already held while other threads want it. Linux provides the **futex** system call for this. Its manual page calls it fast user-space locking, because a lock built on it needs no system call at all when it is uncontended, just one atomic instruction. `futex_wait` puts the caller to sleep if a memory word still has an expected value, and `futex_wake` wakes a waiter.

Any read-modify-write (read a value, change it, write it back) of shared data (even `x++`) is several instructions, and a context switch can split them. Protect every critical section with a lock, and build locks on atomic hardware instructions, never on plain loads and stores.

"It is a single line of C" does not make it atomic, and `volatile` does not either: that C keyword only tells the compiler to really load and store the variable on every access instead of keeping it in a register. OSTEP's counter is declared `volatile int` and still loses updates.

blocks.question: Why does the flag-based lock fail while the test-and-set lock works?
options: Test-and-set is faster, so the window for an interrupt is smaller
The flag lock forgets to reset the flag in unlock()
The flag lock only fails on multiprocessors
Test-and-set reads the old value and writes the new one as one atomic step, so two threads cannot both see the lock as free
blocks.explain: In the flag lock, a thread can test (see 0) and then be preempted before it sets the flag, letting another thread also see 0. Test-and-set fuses test and set into a single atomic operation. Speed has nothing to do with it, and the failure happens even on one CPU with a timer interrupt.

blocks.question: On a single CPU with a non-preemptive scheduler (no timer switches), Thread 2 calls a spin lock held by Thread 1. What happens?
options: Thread 2 acquires the lock after one time slice
Thread 2 spins forever: Thread 1 never gets the CPU back to release the lock
The lock automatically turns into a sleeping lock
Thread 1 releases the lock because spinning causes an interrupt
blocks.explain: A spinning thread never gives up the CPU on its own. Without preemption, the holder never runs again, so the lock is never released. OSTEP points out that spin locks need a preemptive scheduler to work correctly on a single processor.

lessons.title: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores

blocks.md: Locks give mutual exclusion, but threads also need to *wait* for each other. Tiny example: a parent thread creates a child and must not print "parent: end" until the child has run. The obvious fix is a shared flag: the child sets `done = 1`, and the parent loops `while (done == 0) ;`. OSTEP calls this hugely inefficient: the parent burns CPU spinning, and on one CPU it spins away its whole time slice while the child it waits for cannot run.

A **condition variable** (CV) is an explicit queue that threads put themselves on when some condition is not yet true (waiting), and that another thread, after changing the state, uses to wake one of them (signaling). The idea goes back to Dijkstra's "private semaphores"; Tony Hoare named it a condition variable in work on monitors (a lock bundled with the data it protects and the code that uses it). In POSIX: `pthread_cond_wait(&c, &m)` must be called with mutex `m` held. It releases `m` and puts the caller to sleep as **one atomic step**, and re-acquires `m` before returning. `pthread_cond_signal(&c)` wakes at least one waiting thread, if there is one.

blocks.caption: OSTEP's join with a condition variable (Figure 30.3), inlined. It always prints parent: begin, child, parent: end, whichever thread runs first.

blocks.md: Each piece is needed. Without the state variable `done`: if the child runs first, its signal finds nobody waiting and is simply dropped, and the parent later waits forever. Without the lock: the parent can see `done == 0`, be preempted before it calls wait, and miss the child's signal. OSTEP's rules: hold the lock when you call wait or signal, keep the condition in a state variable, and wait inside a `while` loop.

blocks.title: A lost wakeup without the lock, and the fix

scenes.caption: Broken version, no lock. The parent reads done and sees 0, so it decides to sleep. Before it calls wait(), a timer interrupt switches to the child.
The child sets done = 1 and signals. No thread is waiting yet, so the signal does nothing: a condition variable keeps no memory of past signals.
The parent resumes where it was and calls wait(). It sleeps forever: the only wakeup it could get has already happened.
Fixed version. The parent holds the lock m while it checks done and calls wait(). The child must take m before touching done, so it cannot slip in between.
wait() released m and put the parent to sleep in one atomic step, so the child now gets m, sets done and signals a thread that really is waiting.
Before wait() returns, the parent re-acquires m. Its while loop re-checks done, sees 1 and carries on.

blocks.md: A harder case is the **producer/consumer** or **bounded buffer** problem, first posed by Dijkstra. Producers put items into a fixed-size buffer and consumers take them out. A multi-threaded web server works this way, with requests in a work queue. So does the shell pipe `grep foo file.txt | wc -l`: grep produces lines, wc consumes them, and between them sits a bounded buffer in the kernel. OSTEP starts with a buffer of one slot and a `count` that is 0 (empty) or 1 (full).

blocks.title: Broken bounded buffer: one CV and if (OSTEP Figure 30.9)

scenes.caption: One producer Tp, two consumers Tc1 and Tc2, a one-slot buffer (count is 0 or 1). Tc1 runs first, finds the buffer empty and sleeps at c3, releasing the mutex.
Tp fills the buffer (p4) and signals (p5). That moves Tc1 from sleeping to ready, but Tc1 has not run yet.
Tp unlocks (p6), loops, finds the buffer full and sleeps at p3.
Tc2 sneaks in before Tc1. The buffer is full, so it skips the wait, takes the value (c4) and signals, waking Tp.
Now Tc1 finally runs. It returns from wait at c3 and, because of the if, goes straight to get() at c4. The buffer is empty: the assertion inside get() fires.

blocks.md: The bug: a signal only says the state *may* have changed. Between the wakeup and the moment the woken thread runs, another thread can change it again. This meaning of signal is called **Mesa semantics**, after Mesa, a Xerox PARC programming language whose monitors and condition variables Butler Lampson and David Redell described in 1980, and OSTEP says virtually every system uses it. The stronger **Hoare semantics**, where the woken thread runs immediately, is harder to build. The fix is to replace `if` with `while`, so a woken thread re-checks the condition. The loop also covers *spurious wakeups*, which some thread libraries allow: a thread woken when no signal was meant for it.

blocks.prompt: Change both `if`s to `while`, but keep one condition variable. Two consumers go to sleep, then the producer fills the buffer. Can the program still get stuck?
blocks.reveal: Yes. The producer wakes Tc1 and then sleeps because the buffer is full. Tc1 takes the item and signals, but its signal may wake **Tc2**, the other consumer, instead of the producer. Tc2 finds the buffer empty and sleeps; Tc1 loops and sleeps too. All three are asleep. The fix is **two** condition variables: producers wait on `empty` and signal `fill`, consumers wait on `fill` and signal `empty`, so a consumer can never wake only another consumer.

blocks.caption: OSTEP's working single-slot version (Figure 30.12): while loops and two condition variables. lock, unlock, cond_wait and cond_signal stand for the pthread calls.

blocks.code:
$ ./pc 0     # one CV, if
BUG: get from empty buffer
$ ./pc 1     # one CV, while
stuck: consumed 21 of 200000, count=0
$ ./pc 2     # two CVs, while
all 200000 items consumed
blocks.caption: Real runs of a test program (1 producer, 2 consumers, 200,000 items, a 5 second watchdog) on an Apple Silicon Mac. A second run of each gave the same outcome; the while version got stuck after 2 items.

blocks.md: Dijkstra's **semaphore** does both jobs with one object: an integer value plus two operations. `sem_wait` decrements the value and sleeps if it is now negative; `sem_post` increments it and wakes one waiter if any. When the value is negative, it equals minus the number of waiting threads. Dijkstra called the operations P and V, and later wrote that P comes from *prolaag*, a contraction of the Dutch *probeer* (try) and *verlaag* (decrease), and V from *verhoog* (increase).

blocks.title: A semaphore initialised to 1 is a lock (OSTEP Figure 31.5)

scenes.caption: The value starts at 1: one thread may enter.
T0 calls sem_wait: the value drops to 0, which is not negative, so T0 enters the critical section.
An interrupt switches to T1. Its sem_wait drops the value to -1, which is negative, so T1 sleeps. A negative value counts the waiters.
T0 finishes and calls sem_post: the value rises to 0 and one waiter, T1, is woken.
T1 returns from sem_wait, runs its critical section and posts: the value is back to 1.

blocks.md: The initial value decides the behavior. OSTEP's rule: set it to the number of resources you can hand out right away. A lock has one free slot, so it starts at **1** (a *binary semaphore*). For ordering, such as a parent waiting for a child, nothing is available yet, so it starts at **0**: the child calls `sem_post` when done, and the parent's `sem_wait` returns at once if the child already finished (value 1, back to 0), or sleeps until the post (value -1). Unlike a CV signal, a post is remembered in the value.

Locks are for mutual exclusion; condition variables are for waiting until shared state changes. With a CV, always hold the lock, keep the condition in a state variable, and wait in a while loop. A semaphore can play either role, depending on its initial value.
A condition variable has no memory: signaling when nobody waits does nothing. That is why the waiting thread must check a state variable before it sleeps, rather than relying on catching the signal.

blocks.question: A bounded buffer has one producer and two consumers, one condition variable, and consumers that check `if (count == 0)` before waiting. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing: with a lock held, if and while behave the same
A woken consumer can find the buffer already emptied by the other consumer and call get() on an empty buffer
The producer can overwrite a full buffer even with one consumer
The program deadlocks because wait() keeps the mutex
blocks.explain: Under Mesa semantics a wakeup is only a hint. Between the producer's signal and Tc1 running, Tc2 can take the item. With if, Tc1 does not re-check and calls get() on an empty buffer. wait() releases the mutex while sleeping, so the last option is wrong.

blocks.question: A parent creates a child thread and calls `sem_wait(&s)` to wait until the child calls `sem_post(&s)` as its last action. What must `s` be initialised to?
options: The number of threads
blocks.explain: Nothing is available until the child finishes, so the value starts at 0. If the parent waits first, the value goes to -1 and it sleeps until the post. If the child posts first, the value goes to 1 and the parent's wait returns at once. Starting at 1 would let the parent continue before the child has done anything.

blocks.question: Why does `pthread_cond_wait` take the mutex as an argument?
options: So it can release the mutex and put the thread to sleep as one atomic step, then re-acquire it before returning
So the woken thread is guaranteed to run before any other thread
Because condition variables are implemented as mutexes
So it can free the mutex permanently once the condition is true
blocks.explain: If the thread released the mutex itself and then slept, a signal could arrive in the gap and be lost. Doing both atomically closes that window. Waking does not guarantee running first: that would be Hoare semantics, and pthreads uses Mesa semantics.

lessons.title: Concurrency bugs: atomicity, ordering and deadlock

blocks.md: What do real concurrency bugs look like? OSTEP leans on a study by Shan Lu and colleagues (published at ASPLOS, a systems research conference, in 2008) of bugs found and fixed in four big programs: the MySQL database, the Apache web server, the Mozilla browser and the OpenOffice suite. Of 105 bugs, 74 were **non-deadlock** bugs and 31 were deadlocks.

blocks.title: Concurrency bugs found in four applications (Lu et al., 2008)

scenes.caption: Non-deadlock bugs in each application: 74 in total.
Deadlock bugs: 31 in total. Most real concurrency bugs are not deadlocks.

blocks.md: The first kind is the **atomicity violation**. Lu et al. define it as: "The desired serializability among multiple memory accesses is violated", that is, a code region is meant to be atomic but nothing enforces it. Serializable means the result is as if the regions ran one after another. The MySQL example below checks a pointer and then uses it.

blocks.title: An atomicity violation found in MySQL (OSTEP Figure 32.2)

scenes.caption: Thread 1 checks that proc_info is not NULL. The check passes.
An interrupt switches to Thread 2, which sets proc_info to NULL.
Thread 1 resumes and passes NULL to fputs, which dereferences it: crash. The check and the use were meant to be atomic, but nothing enforced it.

blocks.caption: The fix (OSTEP Figure 32.3): one lock around every access to the field, so the check and the use run as one unit.

blocks.md: The second kind is the **order violation**, defined by Lu et al. as "The desired order between two (groups of) memory accesses is flipped": A should always run before B, but nothing enforces it. OSTEP's Mozilla example: Thread 1's `init()` creates a thread and stores its handle in `mThread`; the new thread's first line reads `mThread->State`. If the new thread runs before the assignment, it reads `mThread` while it is still NULL and crashes. The fix is the previous lesson's pattern: a state variable `mtInit`, a lock and a condition variable, with the new thread waiting in a while loop until `mtInit` is 1. In Lu's study, 97% of non-deadlock bugs were one of these two kinds.

Now **deadlock**: each thread in a group holds a lock and waits for one that another thread in the group holds, so none can proceed. The classic case is two threads taking two locks in opposite orders. It happens only if a context switch lands in the wrong place, which is why it can pass every test and still strike in production.

blocks.title: Two threads, two locks, opposite order

scenes.caption: Thread 1 runs lock(L1) then lock(L2); Thread 2 runs lock(L2) then lock(L1). Thread 1 takes L1, then a context switch happens.
Thread 2 takes L2 and now asks for L1, which Thread 1 holds. Thread 2 blocks.
Thread 1 runs again and asks for L2, held by Thread 2. Now each waits for the other: a cycle in the graph. Neither can ever run again.
Fix: both threads take L1 first. A thread waiting for L1 holds nothing, so whoever holds L1 can always get L2 and finish. No cycle can form.

blocks.caption: Core of a test: main starts both threads and prints how many critical sections ran each second.

blocks.md: Running that test on an Apple Silicon Mac three times, the opposite-order version completed 570, 1,099 and 514 critical sections in its first second and then 0 forever after: deadlocked within the first second. Changing `t2` to take L1 first, as `t1` does, ran tens of millions of critical sections per second without stopping.

Why do deadlocks happen when the fix looks so simple? In big systems, components depend on each other in circles: the virtual memory system may call the file system to page in a block, and the file system may ask the virtual memory system for a page. And encapsulation hides locks: OSTEP's example is Java's `Vector.addAll`. `v1.addAll(v2)` locks v1 and then v2, so a concurrent `v2.addAll(v1)` takes the same two locks in the opposite order, and the caller never sees a lock.

Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani (1971) listed **four conditions** that must all hold for deadlock:

1. **Mutual exclusion**: threads claim exclusive control of resources, such as locks.
2. **Hold-and-wait**: threads hold resources while waiting for more.
3. **No preemption**: resources cannot be forcibly taken away.
4. **Circular wait**: a cycle of threads exists, each holding a resource the next one wants.

Break any one and deadlock is impossible. Prevention is not the only option: some systems instead detect deadlock (look for a cycle among waiting threads) and recover, for example a database aborting one transaction.

Prevention, condition by condition. *Circular wait*: give the locks a fixed order and always acquire in that order. OSTEP calls this the most practical technique; Linux's memory-mapping code documents its order in a comment at the top of mm/filemap.c, for example "i_mmap_rwsem before private_lock before swap_lock before the i_pages lock". *Hold-and-wait*: take all locks at once under one global lock, which costs concurrency. *No preemption*: use `pthread_mutex_trylock`, and on failure release what you hold and start over. Two threads can then keep retrying in lockstep without progress, called **livelock**; a random delay before retrying makes that unlikely. *Mutual exclusion*: lock-free data structures built on atomic instructions such as compare-and-swap (store a new value only if the old one is still what you expect) avoid locks altogether.

blocks.caption: OSTEP's tip for a function such as do_something(m1, m2): use the locks' addresses as the global order. This version takes the higher address first; increasing order works equally well, as long as every thread uses the same rule.

blocks.md: Most concurrency bugs are atomicity violations (fix: a lock around the whole check-then-act) or order violations (fix: a condition variable on a state variable). Deadlock needs four conditions; the usual cure is to acquire locks in one global order.
A deadlock-prone program can run correctly many times, because the deadlock needs an unlucky interleaving. Testing does not show it is safe; a lock order does.

blocks.question: A team makes every thread acquire locks in increasing address order. Which deadlock condition does that remove?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold-and-wait
No preemption
Circular wait
blocks.explain: Threads still hold locks exclusively, still hold one while waiting for the next, and locks still cannot be taken away. But a cycle would need some thread to hold a higher lock while waiting for a lower one, which the order forbids, so circular wait cannot form.

blocks.question: Thread A starts thread B and then sets `cfg = load_config()`. Thread B begins by reading `cfg->port`. It crashes occasionally. What kind of bug is this, and what is the usual fix?
options: An atomicity violation; wrap the read of cfg->port in a lock
An order violation; make B wait on a condition variable until A sets a flag after loading cfg
A deadlock; acquire locks in a global order
A data race on port; declare cfg volatile
blocks.explain: B assumes A's assignment has already happened: the intended order is not enforced. A lock alone does not fix it, since B could still take the lock first and see NULL. B must wait for a state variable (set by A after loading) using a condition variable, as in OSTEP's Mozilla fix. volatile does not create ordering.

blocks.question: Two threads use the trylock protocol: lock L1, trylock L2, and on failure unlock L1 and start over. The other thread does the same with L2 first. What new problem can appear?
options: Livelock: both keep backing off and retrying without either making progress
Deadlock, because trylock blocks
Starvation of the scheduler
Mutual exclusion is lost
blocks.explain: trylock never blocks, so a thread waiting for the second lock never holds the first one for long and deadlock cannot form. But both threads can repeatedly grab one lock each, fail, release and retry in step: livelock. OSTEP suggests a random delay before retrying.

lessons.title: Persistence: how a hard disk spends its time

blocks.md: The third piece is keeping data across power loss. On a hard disk drive (HDD), data sits on spinning platters. Each surface is divided into concentric rings called tracks, each track into 512-byte sectors, and a head on a moving arm reads and writes them. Reading a random block takes three steps: **seek** (move the arm to the right track), **rotation** (wait for the sector to spin under the head) and **transfer** (read the bits).

blocks.caption: The time for one I/O is seek time plus rotation time plus transfer time, and the I/O rate R is the bytes transferred divided by that total time.

blocks.md: OSTEP compares two Seagate drives. The Cheetah 15K.5 spins at 15,000 RPM (revolutions per minute), seeks in 4 ms on average and transfers at up to 125 MB/s. The Barracuda spins at 7,200 RPM, seeks in 9 ms and transfers at 105 MB/s. A minute is 60,000 ms, so one rotation of the Cheetah takes $60000/15000 = 4$ ms. On average the wanted sector is half a rotation away, so average rotational delay is half that: $60000/15000/2 = 2$ ms for the Cheetah and $60000/7200/2 \approx 4.17$ ms for the Barracuda.

blocks.prompt: For a random 4 KB read on the Cheetah: seek 4 ms, rotation 2 ms, transfer $0.004\ \text{MB} / 125\ \text{MB/s} = 0.032$ ms. What throughput does that give?
blocks.reveal: $T_{I/O} = 6.032$ ms, so $R_{I/O} = 0.004\ \text{MB} / 6.032\ \text{ms} \approx 0.66$ MB/s, about 0.5% of the drive's 125 MB/s peak. Almost all the time is mechanical positioning. The Barracuda is worse: 13.2 ms per read, about 0.30 MB/s (OSTEP rounds to 0.31).

blocks.title: Random 4 KB reads versus one sequential 100 MB read

scenes.caption: Random 4 KB reads: 0.66 and 0.30 MB/s. Each tiny read pays a full seek plus half a rotation.
Sequential 100 MB: one seek and rotation, then 800 ms (Cheetah) or 952 ms (Barracuda) of transfer. Totals 806 and 966 ms give 124.1 and 103.6 MB/s.
The ratio is about 187x for the Cheetah and 342x for the Barracuda. Hence OSTEP's tip: use disks sequentially, or at least in large chunks.

blocks.title: Disk throughput as the request size grows

scenes.caption: Cheetah model (4 ms seek, 2 ms rotation, 125 MB/s). Throughput only approaches the peak once each request is megabytes long, so positioning cost is amortized.
Barracuda model (9 ms seek, 4.17 ms rotation, 105 MB/s). Slower positioning pushes the curve right: you need even bigger requests. Simplified: ignores caches and request scheduling.

blocks.md: Because positioning dominates, the OS chooses the order of pending requests. **SSTF** (shortest seek time first) serves the request on the nearest track next; the OS sees only block numbers, so in practice it uses *nearest-block-first*. Its flaw is starvation: a steady stream of nearby requests can postpone a far one forever. The **elevator** algorithm, SCAN, sweeps the head across the disk in one direction, serving requests in track order, then turns around; requests behind the head wait for the next sweep, so none starves. C-SCAN (circular SCAN) sweeps one way only, then jumps back, which is fairer to the outer and inner tracks. Modern drives also schedule internally: the OS issues a few requests at once and the drive, which knows the exact head position, orders them.

Flash **SSDs** (solid-state drives) have no arm and no platter, so there is no seek and no rotation. Writing is the awkward part: a flash *page* (a few KB, for example 4 KB) can be programmed only after its whole *erase block* (typically 128 KB or 256 KB) is erased, which takes milliseconds, and each erase wears the block a little. SSDs hide this behind a *flash translation layer* that writes new data log-style into fresh pages. In OSTEP's table, a Samsung 840 Pro SSD reads 103 MB/s randomly and 421 MB/s sequentially; a Seagate Savvio 15K.3 hard drive manages about 2 and 223. These are drives from about 2013; current NVMe SSDs are many times faster, but small random I/O still trails large sequential I/O, so large sequential I/O still pays off.

A random disk I/O is almost all positioning: seek plus half a rotation, milliseconds, against microseconds of transfer. Make requests large and sequential, and let the scheduler order them by position.

blocks.question: A Cheetah-like disk (4 ms average seek, 2 ms average rotation, 125 MB/s transfer) reads one random 1 MB chunk. Roughly what throughput does it achieve?
options: About 125 MB/s, the peak rate
About 71 MB/s
About 0.66 MB/s, as for 4 KB reads
About 167 MB/s
blocks.explain: Transfer takes 1 MB / 125 MB/s = 8 ms, so the total is 4 + 2 + 8 = 14 ms and the rate is 1 MB / 14 ms, about 71 MB/s. Larger requests amortize the 6 ms of positioning; at 4 KB the same 6 ms dominates and gives 0.66 MB/s.

blocks.question: Why can SSTF (shortest seek time first) starve a request?
options: Because it ignores rotation time
Because the OS does not know the disk's geometry
Because a steady stream of requests near the head always wins, so a request far away may never be served
Because it serves requests in arrival order
blocks.explain: SSTF always picks the closest request. If new nearby requests keep arriving, the far one is never closest. The elevator (SCAN) algorithm fixes this by sweeping in one direction, so every request is reached within a sweep. Ignoring rotation is a real weakness of both, but it is not the cause of starvation.

lessons.title: Files and directories: the API and how vsfs finds your data

blocks.md: Start with `echo hello > foo` and then `cat foo`. Tracing cat's system calls (OSTEP uses `strace` on Linux) shows the whole API in four calls: `open("foo", O_RDONLY)` returns 3, `read(3, buf, 4096)` returns 6 bytes, cat writes them to descriptor 1, a second `read` returns 0, and `close(3)`. To the OS a **file** is just a linear array of bytes with a low-level name, its **inode number**. A **directory** is a file whose contents are a list of (name, inode number) pairs. Directories inside directories form the tree that starts at the root, `/`.

`open()` returns a **file descriptor**: a small integer, private to the process, that names the open file in later calls. In the xv6 teaching kernel it is literally an index into an array in the process structure, `struct file *ofile[NOFILE]`. Every process starts with descriptors 0, 1 and 2 already open (standard input, output and error), so the first file it opens is almost always 3. Each `struct file` entry, part of the system-wide **open file table**, records which inode it refers to, whether it is readable or writable, and the **current offset**.

The offset is where the next read or write starts. Reading or writing N bytes advances it by N. `lseek(fd, offset, whence)` sets it directly: to `offset` (SEEK_SET), the current offset plus `offset` (SEEK_CUR), or the file size plus `offset` (SEEK_END). Two separate `open()`s of one file get two table entries with independent offsets.

blocks.title: One open file, one current offset (OSTEP's traces)

scenes.caption: fd = open("file", O_RDONLY) returns 3. The open file table entry for it starts with current offset 0.
read(fd, buf, 100) returns 100 and moves the offset to 100. The next read continues where this one stopped.
Two more reads return 100 each; the offset reaches 300, the end of the file.
A fourth read returns 0 and the offset stays at 300: end of file. That is how cat knows it is done.
In a fresh open, lseek(fd, 200, SEEK_SET) sets the offset to 200 with no disk I/O at all; read(fd, buf, 50) then returns 50 and leaves it at 250.

blocks.md: `write()` normally just hands data to the file system, which buffers it in memory for a while (OSTEP says perhaps 5 or 30 seconds) before writing it to disk. A program that must know its data is durable, such as a database, calls `fsync(fd)`, which returns only once that file's dirty data is on disk. For a newly created file, the directory that holds it may need an `fsync` too. `rename(old, new)` is usually atomic with respect to crashes: afterwards the file has either the old name or the new one, never something in between. Editors rely on that:

blocks.caption: OSTEP's atomic file update: a crash at any point leaves either the complete old file or the complete new one.

blocks.md: A name is just a directory entry pointing at an inode, so one inode can have several names. `link(old, new)` adds a **hard link**: a new entry with the same inode number. The inode keeps a **link count** of its names. That is why deleting is `unlink()`: it removes one name and decrements the count, and only at zero does the file system free the inode and its blocks. A **symbolic link** (`ln -s`) is different: a small file of its own type whose contents are a path name. It can point to a directory or another file system, which hard links cannot, but it dangles if the target is removed.

blocks.caption: show(name) calls stat() and prints the inode number and link count (st_ino, st_nlink).

blocks.code:
file  inode 109979520, links 1
file  inode 109979520, links 2
file2 inode 109979520, links 2
file  does not exist
file2 inode 109979520, links 1
blocks.caption: Real output on macOS (APFS, the Apple File System). The inode number differs on every machine; the link counts do not.

blocks.md: A **file system** organizes the disk into blocks. OSTEP's very simple file system (vsfs) uses 64 blocks of 4 KB: block 0 is the **superblock** (sizes, where things are, and a magic number, a fixed value that identifies the file system type), block 1 the **inode bitmap**, block 2 the **data bitmap** (one bit per object: free or in use), blocks 3 to 7 the **inode table**, and blocks 8 to 63 the 56 data blocks.

An **inode** (index node) holds a file's metadata: type, size, owner, permissions, timestamps, and where its data blocks are. With 256-byte inodes, a 4 KB block holds 16, so vsfs's five inode blocks give 80 inodes. Files are named internally by inode number, and finding an inode on disk is pure arithmetic.

blocks.title: Finding inode 32 on disk

scenes.caption: The first 12 of 64 blocks. The inode table starts at block 3, byte address 12 KB.
Offset of inode 32 inside the table: 32 x 256 = 8192 bytes = 8 KB, which is inode-table block 8192 / 4096 = 2.
Byte address 12 KB + 8 KB = 20 KB, disk block 5. Disks address 512-byte sectors, so the file system reads sector 20 x 1024 / 512 = 40.
That 4 KB block holds inodes 32 to 47; inode 32 is the first 256 bytes of it.

blocks.md: How does an inode point to a big file's blocks? The **multi-level index**: a few **direct pointers** (12 is typical), each naming one data block, plus an **indirect pointer** to a block filled with more pointers. With 4 KB blocks and 4-byte disk addresses, an indirect block holds 1024 pointers, so the file can reach $(12 + 1024) \times 4$ KB = 4144 KB. A **double indirect** pointer adds $1024 \times 1024$ more blocks, just over 4 GB in total. The tree is lopsided on purpose: measurements show most files are small (about 2 KB is the most common size), and 12 direct pointers already cover 48 KB. ext2 and ext3 use this scheme; XFS and ext4 use *extents* instead, a start block plus a length.

blocks.prompt: A file uses 12 direct pointers and one indirect pointer, with 4 KB blocks. Where is byte 100,000 found, and how many disk reads reach it if nothing is cached and the inode is already in memory?
blocks.reveal: 100,000 / 4096 = 24.4, so it lies in file block 24 (counting from 0). Blocks 0 to 11 are direct; block 24 is entry 24 - 12 = 12 of the indirect block. Two reads: the indirect block, then the data block.

blocks.md: On disk a directory's data is a list of entries: inode number, record length, name length and name, including `.` (the directory itself) and `..` (its parent). To open a path, the file system walks it from the root, whose inode number must be known in advance because it has no parent. Below, OSTEP's `open("/foo/bar")` on a 12 KB (3-block) file, followed by three reads, assuming nothing is cached and the superblock is already in memory.

blocks.title: Disk I/O for open("/foo/bar") and three reads (OSTEP Figure 40.3)

scenes.caption: Path lookup starts at the root, whose inode number is well known (2 in most UNIX file systems). Read the root inode, then its data: the directory entries, where foo is found.
Read foo's inode, then foo's directory data, which gives bar's inode number. Then read bar's inode: permission check, file descriptor returned. open() cost 5 reads.
Each read(): consult bar's inode for the block's address, read the data block, then write the inode to update its last-access time. Three blocks, three I/Os each. No bitmaps: reads allocate nothing.

blocks.md: Every directory on the path costs at least two reads, its inode and its data, so opening `/1/2/3/.../100/file.txt` would cost hundreds of I/Os. Writing is worse: each write that allocates a block takes five I/Os (read and write the data bitmap, read and write the inode, write the data). File systems therefore cache blocks in memory; modern systems keep file blocks in a **unified page cache** shared with virtual memory, which the later course on stack, heap and virtual memory examines in Linux.

Directories map names to inode numbers; inodes map file offsets to disk blocks; the per-process descriptor and the open file table remember where you are. Path lookup costs disk reads in proportion to the path's depth unless the cache has the blocks.
lseek() never moves the disk head. It only changes the offset stored in the open file table. A disk seek happens later, if the next read or write lands on a different track.

blocks.question: With nothing cached, each directory fitting in one block, and the superblock in memory, how many disk reads does `open("/a/b/c")` cost?
blocks.explain: Root inode, root data, a's inode, a's data, b's inode, b's data, and finally c's inode: 7 reads. open() reads the target's inode but not its data; the data is read by later read() calls.

blocks.question: After `echo hi > file; ln file file2; rm file`, what does `cat file2` print?
options: hi, because file2 is another name for the same inode, whose link count is now 1
Nothing: the data was deleted with file
An error: file2 is a dangling link
hi, because ln copied the file's blocks
blocks.explain: ln creates a hard link: a second directory entry with the same inode number, and the link count goes to 2. rm calls unlink, which removes one name and drops the count to 1, so the inode and data stay. A symbolic link (ln -s) would dangle. No blocks are copied.

blocks.question: An inode has 12 direct pointers and one indirect pointer; blocks are 4 KB and disk addresses 4 bytes. What is the largest file it can describe?
options: 48 KB
4 MB exactly
4 GB
blocks.explain: The indirect block holds 4096 / 4 = 1024 pointers. Together with the 12 direct ones that is 1036 blocks of 4 KB = 4144 KB. 48 KB is only the direct part; 4 GB needs a double indirect pointer.

blocks.md: Updating a file usually means writing several blocks, and the disk commits one write at a time. Power can fail between any two. OSTEP's running example is appending one 4 KB block to a file in vsfs. The goal is to move the disk from one consistent state to the next **atomically**, all or nothing, even though the writes land one by one. This is the **crash-consistency problem**.

blocks.title: Which of the three writes reached the disk?

scenes.caption: Appending one block takes three writes: the inode I[v2] (new size, pointer to block 5), the data bitmap B[v2] (block 5 in use) and the data block Db. A crash can strike between any of them.
Only Db: no inode points to it and the bitmap says free, so it is as if the write never happened. Consistent; the user just lost the data.
Only I[v2]: the inode points to block 5, which still holds old garbage, and the bitmap says block 5 is free. Garbage data and an inconsistency.
Only B[v2]: block 5 is marked used but nothing points to it. Inconsistent: a space leak.
I[v2] and B[v2] but not Db: the metadata agrees with itself, so it looks consistent, yet the file's new block is garbage.
I[v2] and Db without B[v2]: the file reads correctly, but the bitmap still says block 5 is free, so it could be handed out again. B[v2] and Db without I[v2]: used, written, owned by no file.

blocks.md: Early file systems let inconsistencies happen and repaired them at reboot with **fsck** (file system check), which runs before the file system is mounted (attached to the directory tree for use). Its phases: sanity-check the superblock; scan every inode and indirect block to rebuild the bitmaps, trusting the inodes; check each inode's fields; recount every inode's links by walking the whole directory tree, moving inodes no directory names into `lost+found`; find blocks claimed by two inodes; clear pointers outside the disk; and check that directories start with `.` and `..`. fsck cannot fix the inode that points at garbage, since the metadata looks fine. Worse, it is slow: it reads the whole disk to repair an update of three blocks, which on large volumes can take minutes or hours.

**Journaling**, also called **write-ahead logging**, borrows the database idea: before overwriting anything in place, first write a note describing the update to a reserved area, the **journal** (the log). After a crash, recovery reads only the small journal instead of the whole disk. The first file system to do it was Cedar's, at Xerox PARC in 1987; Linux ext3 and ext4, IBM's JFS, SGI's XFS and Windows NTFS all journal.

The note is a **transaction**: a group of writes that must take effect all or nothing. It begins with a **TxB** (transaction begin) block holding a transaction identifier (TID) and the final addresses of the blocks, then the new blocks themselves, I[v2], B[v2] and Db, and ends with a **TxE** (transaction end) block. Once the transaction is safely in the journal, the file system **checkpoints**: it writes the blocks to their real locations. Logging the data block Db too, not only the metadata, is called **data journaling**.

The protocol has a deliberate wait: the file system issues TxB and the contents, waits for them to complete, and only then issues TxE (a quiz at the end of this lesson asks why). The disk guarantees that a single 512-byte sector is written completely or not at all, so TxE is made one sector and the commit is atomic. Linux ext4 adds a checksum of the transaction to the begin and end blocks, an idea from Vijayan Prabhakaran: recovery spots a torn transaction by the mismatch, so all five writes can be issued at once.

blocks.prompt: A crash hits after TxE is on disk but before any checkpoint write. After reboot, is the append lost?
blocks.reveal: No. Recovery scans the journal, finds the committed transaction and replays it, writing its blocks to their final locations. Because the journal holds the new contents, this is called **redo logging**. If some checkpoint writes had already landed, writing them again is harmless. A transaction without a valid TxE is simply skipped, leaving the old consistent state.

blocks.md: The journal has a fixed size, so it is used as a **circular log**. Once a transaction is checkpointed, its space can be reused: a small header, the **journal superblock**, records the oldest and newest transactions not yet checkpointed. That adds a fourth step, **free**. ext3 also buffers many updates into one global transaction, so blocks touched by several operations are logged once rather than once per operation.

blocks.title: Data journaling, then where a crash lands
